strengths: Addresses critical gap in NLP for underrepresented Indian languages covering 10 languages across 5 scripts
Comprehensive and practical contribution with monolingual, bilingual, and multilingual model variants
Demonstrates efficient deployment with CPU-only inference, showing competitive performance with models 20-64x larger
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ARC, MMLU, HellaSwag, XNLI, XCOPA, etc.) and human evaluation
Novel mBharat tokenizer achieves competitive/superior fertility scores compared to LLaMa-3.1, Gemma-2, and GPT-4o
Significant resource contributions including 23k instruction-tuning datasets per language for 5 languages
Well-motivated typological grouping strategy for multilingual pretraining to avoid curse of multilinguality
Practical value through demonstration of various downstream capabilities (grammar correction, poetry, summarization, etc.)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: RoPE scaling method is straightforward (context_length / max_permissible_length) lacking mathematical formulation and theoretical justification; tokenizer combines existing BPE and Unigram techniques; missing ablation studies

Significant human evaluation limitations: only 3 of 10 languages evaluated (Bangla, Hindi, Sanskrit); missing critical details (annotator count, inter-annotator agreement, detailed guidelines); no statistical significance testing

Unfair baseline comparisons: GPT-3.5-Turbo comparisons problematic as Figures 4-5 show complete failures on Indian text, suggesting model doesn't support these languages; comparing models trained on different data/compute budgets without controls

Benchmark evaluation concerns: uses machine-translated versions of standard benchmarks (ARC, MMLU, HellaSwag) which may introduce translation artifacts; no perplexity comparisons with baselines; unexplained anomalies (performance drops in few-shot settings, Table 4)

Critical reproducibility deficits: no information on code/model release; incomplete architecture details (embedding dim, layers, heads, FFN); RoPE scaling cannot be reproduced from description; tokenizer training procedure underspecified

Data and experimental design issues: unusual 95%-5% train-val split with minimal validation data; dramatic token count imbalance across languages (26.2B-66B) not addressed; instruction dataset is heterogeneous mix (5k human, 15k Google-translated, 3k self-instruct) without quality analysis

Missing analysis depth: no explanation for extreme perplexity variation across languages (1.75 for Sanskrit vs. 16.99 for Hindi 162M); limited language transfer analysis; absent error analysis and discussion of failure modes; no evaluation of translation quality impact

Presentation and scope limitations: human-evaluated samples appear cherry-picked; no significance testing across benchmark results (many differences <2%); missing discussion of ethical considerations, data biases, and limitations; incomplete related work on position-based scaling techniques

strengths: Addresses important problem of developing accessible language models for low-resource Indian languages with social value
Practical engineering contributions: models are genuinely efficient, trainable on single GPU with CPU-only inference
Comprehensive coverage: 10+ models across multiple languages, scripts, and configurations (monolingual, bilingual, multilingual)
mBharat tokenizer achieves lower fertility scores than LLaMa-3.1, Gemma2, and GPT-4o, providing useful optimization
Multiple evaluation approaches including quantitative benchmarks and human evaluation
Creation of 23k instruction datasets for multiple languages is a useful resource contribution
weaknesses: Critical issue: claims of outperforming GPT-3.5-Turbo (175B) with 100-360M models lack rigor—based on limited human evaluation of 3 languages with no inter-annotator agreement, evaluator counts, or set sizes reported
Human evaluation methodology severely underdescribed: no protocol details, sample sizes, inter-rater agreement metrics, or clear definitions of evaluation criteria
Unfair benchmark comparisons: Paramanu models trained on significantly fewer tokens (26.21B for Bangla) than baselines (340B for BLOOM), making direct comparison fundamentally problematic
Questionable evaluation on translated English benchmarks may not validly assess language understanding in Indian languages
Unexplained performance anomalies: Sanskrit perplexity substantially outperforms Hindi despite less data; n-shot evaluation shows consistent degradation from 0-shot to 25-shot setting

Limited technical novelty: RoPE scaling lacks theoretical justification and appears to be straightforward scaling; tokenizer uses standard BPE+Unigram; typological grouping is sound engineering, not novel methodology
RoPE scaling method insufficiently explained—how dividing context length by maximum permissible size fundamentally solves memory constraints is unclear
No statistical rigor: missing error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or p-values for claims like 'outperformed by X%'

Reproducibility concerns: no mention of code/model availability, vague corpus descriptions (no total sizes or deduplication details), missing hyperparameters (learning rate, optimizer, warmup, dropout)
Instruction-tuning dataset construction issues: mixing human annotations with Google Translate and self-instruct without quality analysis or task diversity validation
Reads as technical report rather than research paper: limited analysis of why models work well, no error analysis or case studies, missing qualitative insights
Missing dedicated related work section and discussion of limitations, potential biases, generalization concerns, and ethical considerations

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem—efficient LLMs for Indian languages serving 1+ billion speakers, with practical deployability on limited hardware (single GPU, CPU inference)

Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation strategy combining perplexity, multiple zero-shot benchmarks (MMLU, ARC, XCOPA, XNLI, etc.), and human evaluation across grammar, coherence, creativity, and factuality for 3 languages
Strong empirical results demonstrating Paramanu models outperform 7B-scale models (Bloom, LLaMa, GPT-3.5-Turbo, OPT, GPT-J) on human evaluation despite being 20-64× smaller

mBharat tokenizer is a substantive contribution with demonstrated advantages (fertility score 1.25 for Hindi vs. LLaMa/Gemma/GPT-4o), with useful capability to tokenize unseen languages in the same script

Thoughtful methodological design choices including typological grouping for multilingual pretraining, language-specific and domain-specific tokenization strategies, and comparable corpora selection grounded in linguistic principles
Ambitious scope creating a coherent family of models (monolingual, bilingual, multilingual) at multiple scales (13.29M-367.5M parameters) across 10 Indian languages and 5 scripts
Novel RoPE embedding scaling approach enabling efficient context expansion on single GPUs, demonstrating that high-quality models don't require massive compute resources
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—uses standard Transformer decoder-only architecture; primary contributions are engineering/application-level rather than algorithmic innovations suited for top venues

RoPE scaling method insufficiently validated: appears ad-hoc (simple division by max_permissible_context_size), lacks theoretical justification, has no ablation studies on scaling factors, and missing comparison with alternative efficient context extension methods (ALiBi, etc.)

Human evaluation has critical limitations: covers only 3 languages (Bangla, Hindi, Sanskrit), sample sizes not clearly stated, inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ) not reported, and comparison with ChatGPT potentially unfair due to different instruction-tuning protocols

Missing essential ablation studies: no isolation of tokenization strategy contributions (BPE vs. Unigram), no comparison of typological grouping vs. standard multilingual pretraining, and RoPE scaling sensitivity not studied

Multilingual transfer phenomenon observed but not rigorously analyzed—no investigation of linguistic properties enabling transfer, mParamanu results mixed with sometimes underperformance vs. specialized models, and comparable corpora handling claims not validated

Dataset descriptions inadequate: limited details on corpus composition/sizes/sources, no verification of quality or discussion of potential biases, data balancing across languages unclear, and ethical considerations for data collection unaddressed

Reproducibility concerns: model/code availability not explicitly stated, hyperparameter choices lack justification, training dynamics (loss curves, convergence) not shown, preprocessing details sparse, instruction-tuning dataset composition unclear, no random seed reporting

Benchmark evaluation lacks rigor: translated benchmark quality not discussed, perplexity comparisons problematic across different training protocols, no statistical significance testing, modest improvements in many zero-shot results (1-2%), and baselines not specifically optimized for Indian languages

Limited generalization analysis: no evaluation on code-switched text, unseen language transfer not rigorously tested, cross-script transfer unexplored, failure case analysis missing, and error patterns not analyzed
Statistical rigor absent: no confidence intervals or significance tests on benchmark results, human evaluation lacks statistical analysis, inference speed comparisons lack variance/confidence bounds

Presentation issues: dense paper with underdeveloped claims, frequent use of 'novel' without differentiation, mathematical formulation of RoPE scaling not explicit, some overclaiming (e.g., 'most advanced'), and related work could better position contributions

Instruction-tuning limited in scope: only 5 languages instruction-tuned, 23k instructions per language modest by current standards, machine-translated instruction quality not validated, and beneficial instruction types not analyzed

strengths: Addresses critical gap in low-resource NLP for 1.4 billion Indian language speakers with practical resource efficiency (<$1,000 training budget on single GPU)
Comprehensive evaluation across 21 baseline models with multiple benchmarks, ablation studies, human evaluation (κ=0.85-0.87), and cross-lingual transfer analysis
Strong open-science contribution with publicly released models, tokenizers, and instruction-tuning datasets enabling reproducibility and community use
Hybrid Unigram+BPE tokenization shows consistent improvements (1-2% benchmarks, superior fertility scores) with clear morphological benefits demonstrated in Table 7
Efficient empirical results: outperforms all LLMs <3B parameters and competitive with 3-8B models while being 10-100× smaller and trained on 50-100× less data
Thorough data preprocessing pipeline (language identification, deduplication, toxicity filtering, script-specific handling) and instruction-tuning with quality guidelines (Fleiss Kappa 0.87)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: tokenization combines existing methods (Bostrom & Durrett 2020), RoPE scaling adapted from Chen et al. (2023); core contribution is engineering/domain application rather than algorithmic innovation

Fundamental data constraints significantly limit capabilities: 54.6GB (25-66B tokens) is 50-100× less than competitive models; limited domain diversity causes weak MMLU performance (often below random baseline for Tamil/Telugu), indicating knowledge gaps

Evaluation concerns: zero-shot only (no task-specific fine-tuning), 1024-token context length, weak knowledge benchmarks, and overstated claims (e.g., 'outperforms most larger models' only true for <3B models)
Instruction-tuning dataset too small (23K examples) with quality degradation from machine translation (8-13% WER); modest improvements (1-4% most languages); limited analysis of practical utility
Unexplained n-shot degradation (Table 14) where performance drops 0→25 shot, suggesting weak in-context learning ability; unclear why Telugu differs from other languages
Training convergence not verified: models trained with GPU interruptions over 42-239 hours, hyperparameter transfer robustness via μP not validated, detailed training logs omitted
Safety deficits: no safety mechanisms despite acknowledging models generate 'factually incorrect, biased, inappropriate content'; non-commercial license limits adoption compared to open alternatives
Model capability limitations: low CPU inference speeds (12-42 tokens/sec), unclear real-world deployment readiness, no task-specific application examples beyond benchmarks

strengths: Addresses important problem of language representation for ~1.4B speakers of Indian languages
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 5 languages and 20+ baseline models with multiple benchmarks
Practical contribution with open-source models, tokenizers, and datasets enabling community adoption
Linguistically motivated hybrid BPE+Unigram tokenizer with clear examples of morphological preservation
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating value of tokenization and data cleaning choices
Accessible design under $1000 budget on single GPU enables under-resourced researchers
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: tokenizer is straightforward combination of existing methods; RoPE interpolation directly applies Chen et al. (2023) without methodological innovation
Unfair experimental comparisons: models trained on vastly different data (Paramanu-Hindi: 66B tokens vs Sarvam 2B: 4T tokens, 60× more) compared without controlling for training budget
Overstated claims relative to actual results: claim 'outperforms most larger models' contradicted by poor performance vs Llama-3.2, Aya23-8B, Bloomz-7B on many benchmarks
Weak absolute performance on key benchmarks: Bangla MMLU ~25% (random baseline); heavy instruction-tuning dependence (Hindi +9% gain) suggests weak base model quality
Machine-translated instruction data quality unverified: 15K instructions from Google Translate with acknowledged below-human accuracy, 8-13% error rates in manual corrections, no impact analysis
N-shot performance degradation (Table 14) shows concerning drops inconsistent with competitiveness claims; inadequately investigated
No convergence verification despite frequent GPU interruptions during training; single A100 may be insufficient
Insufficient failure analysis: no investigation of error types, which tasks fail, language-specific challenges, or explanation for variable instruction-tuning gains
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing; single evaluation run without repetition
Limited domain coverage by design: explicitly excludes scientific journals, legal documents, specialized texts—acknowledged to cause weak performance
Incomplete technical analysis: position interpolation results show inconsistent optima (Table 5) without explanation; hyperparameter transfer via μP not verified; ablation limited
Cross-lingual transfer claims overstated: interesting observations (Sanskrit→Hindi transfer, Marathi-Hindi matching) lack rigorous analysis
Reproducibility concerns: multiple missing links ('Available at: [incomplete]' appears 3+ times); dependent on author code/data release
Presentation issues: abstract dense and difficult to parse; overstated language ('competitive,' 'strong') relative to actual numbers; important limitations relegated to end

strengths: Addresses critical gap: First open-source monolingual LLMs for 5 major Indian languages serving 1.4 billion speakers with realistic resource constraints (single GPU, <$1000)
Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated on 21 comparison models across 7+ benchmarks per language with human evaluation (κ=0.85-0.79), strong ablations, and detailed analysis
Strong empirical results: Outperforms all <3B parameter models on each language; 108M Bangla model competitive with Sarvam 2B (20× smaller); 367M Hindi rivals 7B models
Excellent reproducibility: Open-source models/tokenizers/datasets, detailed hyperparameters, training logs, CPU inference speed, and transparent methodology documentation

Principled technical contributions: Morphology-aligned hybrid BPE+Unigram tokenizer with linguistic motivation; RoPE position interpolation enabling long-sequence training on single GPU; high-quality instruction datasets with inter-annotator agreement κ=0.87
Demonstrates important finding: Small, well-designed monolingual models outperform larger multilingual baselines for low-resource languages, challenging 'scale-everything-up' paradigm
Honest limitations discussion: Transparent about convergence constraints, machine translation quality, lack of safety mechanisms, and dataset domain limitations
Methodologically sound: Follows Chinchilla scaling laws, standard transformer architecture appropriately, systematic data cleaning, and principled hyperparameter choices via μP transfer
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Hybrid tokenizer adapts Bostrom & Durrett (2020) with modest 1-2% improvements; RoPE scaling is straightforward linear interpolation adapting Chen et al. (2023); no comparison with other morphology-aware approaches (morphological segmentation, sentencepiece regularization, byte-level models)

Instruction-tuning quality concerns: Machine-translated Tamil/Telugu instructions with no manual post-editing achieve only 1-2% gains versus 9% for Hindi, undermining claims of competitive instruction-tuned models across all languages

Convergence limitations: 100K training steps on single GPU with 54.6GB total data (order of magnitude smaller than GPT-3) and repeated-epoch training increase overfitting risk; unclear if models have converged

Evaluation scope limitations: Zero-shot only; no task-specific fine-tuning; limited to reading comprehension/commonsense (missing generation); human evaluation on only 2 languages with 10 prompts; n-shot degradation (Table 14) contradicts LLM findings and is unexplained

RoPE scaling analysis insufficient: Table 5 shows non-monotonic improvements (Telugu α=1→2→3 varies 31.75→33.22→31.87); no investigation of actual long-range dependency learning or whether models utilize extended context

Cross-lingual transfer underanalyzed: Sanskrit experiment feels exploratory; asymmetric Marathi↔Hindi transfer explained as 'reverse transfer' without theoretical grounding; mParamanu underperforms monolingual counterparts, suggesting multilinguality curse left unexplored

Comparison fairness issues: Context length variations uncontrolled (1024 vs. 2048-8192 baselines); some baseline results sourced from papers without verification; Sarvam 2B trained on 50× more tokens insufficiently caveated

Incomplete tokenization analysis: Table 7 examples are cherry-picked; missing quantitative morpheme boundary detection accuracy; no corpus-level token/word statistics despite fertility metric in Figure 1
